utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. May I have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and the case manager, Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Defence of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, myself, Edina Residovic, lead counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Defence of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Mr. Ibrisimovic, and Mr. Mulalic. Also on behalf of the accused Kubura, I should like to thank the Court and the Trial Chamber and my colleagues from the Prosecution, and especially the staff of the registrar, who put in a great deal of time to allow the accused to attend his mother's funeral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This afternoon's hearing has commenced. The Chamber would like to greet all those present, Mr. Withopf and Mr. Mundis of the OTP, the Defence counsels and the accused, and General Kubura actually will be arriving shortly, because he had the death of his mother that overtook him and he was authorised to attend the funeral of his mother. And that is the reason why he is not in court today. But I hope that he will be here tomorrow. And in keeping with the proceedings and Rules, he will be represented by his Defence counsel and they will inform him of today's hearing. Today we have a video conference lined up and two witnesses for it. But I should first of all like to give the floor to Mr. Withopf, and I think we can go into private session for that. Mr. Registrar, may be go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. ZK, would it be correct to say that the relations between the Croat and Muslim neighbours before the conflict in 1993 were very good? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Immediately after the attack on Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992, the attack that was carried out by the JNA and the Serbian Armed Forces, immediately after that attack the Muslims and the Croats from your village fought together; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Serbian forces were positioned above your village on the Vlasic Mountain, and at the end of May and the beginning of June 1992 they shelled Maljine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of 1992, the Muslims and the Croats held the lines facing the Serbian forces on Mount Vlasic. They were together. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. ZK, would it be correct to say that the Muslim soldiers or members of the BH army, in order to reach their positions on Vlasic, passed through the Croatian part of the village, as that was the shortest route to the positions facing the Serbian forces? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. ZK, you weren't an HVO member but you do know that men who were fit for military service were HVO members. They were members of the Frankopan Brigade, whose headquarters were in Guca Gora. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. ZK, would it be correct to say that in April 1993, the men from your village who were HVO members stopped going to the lines on Vlasic and guards were organised and defence around the village in the direction of places where the BH army was? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, on Vlasic, some remained. They were together, and they then withdrew gradually, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Would it be correct to say that the person who organised the defence of your village was Bozo Djakovic? He was the main person in charge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were a number of persons. There was Bozo and there was Stanko Juric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now go into private session again, as I want the ask the witness a number of questions that could reveal his identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. ZK, would it be correct to say that the intensive fighting in your village started early on the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they started -- the fighting started at 3.30. They first started shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point in time -- I apologise. I'll rephrase that question. I'll ask you this question in private session. But there is another question I would like to put to you now: Would it be correct to say that the HVO lines, which had previously been established facing the BH army lines, were soon penetrated and HVO soldiers withdrew in the direction of the village and some of them also went towards the clinic? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're continuing the proceedings, and I turn towards the Prosecution to hear about the second witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, since I'm going to apply for protective measures for the second witness, could we please go into private session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Private session, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness ZL, do you still recall the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. I went to the village. This happened in the morning. They captured us. This is what happened. I was in prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness ZL, let's go step by step. What happened in the morning of the 8th of June, 1993? What happened to you and what happened to Maljine, if anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was an attack, a fierce attack. We were captured and then taken to prison in the direction of Mehurici. As we were going towards Mehurici, there was a group and they separated the young people and sent them back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Witness ZL. Let's first address the attack on the 8th of June, 1993. Who was attacking -- which army was attacking the village of Maljine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslim one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness ZL, what actually did you notice once the Muslim army attacked the village of Maljine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I saw shooting. They shouted out. They went to the village. We were in shelters. They told us to surrender. We surrendered. And they captured us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, Witness ZL, let's go step by step. Once the Muslim army attacked the village of Maljine, did you see any houses burning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please inform the Trial Chamber whose houses you have seen burning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Juric's house, in the hamlet of Vranjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Witness ZL, did you see any other houses burning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Up where an artillery shell fell, in Maljine, Medukic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your recollection, were there any further houses you've seen burning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw stables burning, two of them, Stipo Djakovic and Kramar's stables.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall or have you seen who made the houses and the stables burning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who the troops were. It was the Muslims. It wasn't us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for clarification, Witness ZL, was it the Muslim army which made the houses in Maljine burning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did happen, to your recollection, Witness ZL, to your own house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of my houses burnt down and my stables. When they took us to Mehurici, I saw that too. My brother's house burnt down and his stables. Tavic Smilja's house was on fire. Marko Juric's and Drago Juric's houses, they both burnt down. Vuric Sprana's [phoen] house burnt down. Kate Saric's house burnt down. They were all in flames at that morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness ZL, at the time you were taken to Mehurici - and we will address this later on - but at the time you were taken to Mehurici, was there still firing ongoing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to having been taken to Mehurici on the 8th of June, 1993, Witness ZL, did you have an opportunity to go back to your own house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. As we weren't in one shelter - we were kept in two or three shelters - in one shelter, some people were captured. I heard that a relative of mine was looking for her daughter. I didn't know about this. But when they captured me, I asked if I could go home to see whether the girl was down there. A commander turned up. A soldier went down with me. When we got there, there were soldiers on the floors looking for things, and things were outside on the road. I saw that the girl wasn't there. I then returned and set off in the direction of Mehurici again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness ZL, what were the things about that were outside on the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was the bicycle, there was coffee, there was tobacco, there were -- there was a device. There was flour. There were various things. They took what they could carry. They couldn't carry the bed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were the owners of the items you just detailed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mine. It was my property, taken out of my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please inform the Trial Chamber who took your property out of your house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Muslim troops. We found two soldiers in the house. They were searching in the house, looking for things and taking things outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you, Witness ZL, have you yourself seen the Muslim soldiers taking your things out of your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did, as I went there with this commander of theirs. You could hear a noise on the floor. Two young men came out. He asked them what they were doing. They said they were look for something. And he didn't tell them anything else. They returned. I had a look around. There was nothing I could do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever get your things back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The commander of the Muslim army you were just referring to, did he give you some explanation where he came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he give you some further information in respect to the fact that he came from Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He said, "Don't worry. Nothing will happen to you." I then left him and went off with the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier on, Witness ZL, you were already mentioning that you were taken to Mehurici. How did it happen that you were taken to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just said. One group went off before me. When I returned to my house, we were gathered - there were quite a few of us - and we were then driven off towards Mehurici, down the road towards Mehurici. As we were going towards Mehurici, we came across a group of HVO troops and they sent them back. There were two or three young men. There were sick men. They hadn't served in the army. They then separated us. One of them was a young man. He went to school and his father said, "Don't touch him. He doesn't know anything about all of this." And then they sent him off, too. And they were all shot up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, Witness ZL, let's go step by step. Did you volunteer to go to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't volunteer. Why would I volunteer? I was forced to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Witness ZL, who did force you to go to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Muslim army. They didn't let anyone remain on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of you were forced by the Muslim army to go to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The whole group. There were 257 of us in a hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these 257 individuals, what was their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were just Croats, all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the 257 Croats, were they soldiers or were they civilians or a mixture of both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all civilians. The ones who were there in prison were all civilians. And the others that they took back, they were soldiers and they surrendered. And the others were taken to Bikosi and shot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the time, Witness ZL, when you left for Mehurici -- when you left Maljine for Mehurici on the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't look at my watch. It might have been 9.00 or 10.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it 9.00 or 10.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the morning. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to leaving Maljine, Witness ZL, did you have a look back to the village of Maljine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, before I'd crossed. When you cross, you can't see Maljine any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your recollection, Witness ZL, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to leaving to Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's what I saw. They said, "Surrender." They shouted out "surrender" to us, and that's what happened. We surrendered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time you left for Mehurici, Witness ZL, did you see houses burning in Maljine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've just said. Until we got to Greda, we could. But once we'd crossed Greda, we couldn't. It's the -- we were the other side of Greda, and you couldn't see Maljine any more. We left them behind, behind our backs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for clarification, Witness ZL, whom did you leave behind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just said, Witness ZL, "We left them behind, behind our backs." Whom did you leave behind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When we crossed the other side of Greda or the rock, you couldn't see our village any more. So the other side of Greda.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: We're not quite sure what "Greda" means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then after us, there was this third group that had been captured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier on, Witness ZL, you were mentioning that whilst you were walking to Mehurici you were stopped. Can you please provide us with some more detail, what actually did happen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were stopped because they took the young people away. And there were some people who were masked. And that's why we were held up there, while this separation was taking place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ones who stopped you and the ones who did the separation, Witness ZL, were they soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to what army, to your recollection, did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslim one. I don't know. I didn't follow ranks and stuff. I was beside myself. I was wondering what was going to happen to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The members of the Muslim army who were doing the separation, were they local Muslims or were they foreign Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't see who they were because they had masks on their faces, so you couldn't tell whether they were locals or what. The foreigners, the Arabs, didn't wear masks, whereas the local ones had masks. And so I'm sure they were local people because they had masks on their faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for clarification, Witness ZL, does this, what you just said, mean there were local soldiers of the Muslim army together with foreign soldiers of the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the Mujahedin were with them too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection to this line of questioning on the part of my learned colleague, because the witness on several occasions when asked repeatedly said, "How do I know who they are? I wasn't able to recognise them. They were probably," et cetera, et cetera, "probably locals." Now, the Prosecutor, despite answers of that kind, repeats his question and says that the witness recognised members of the Muslim army among the group, whereas the witness at no point in time gave an answer to that effect. So there were several questions along those lines. They were leading questions and did not follow on from the answers given by the witness previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I can't see any leading questions. I actually went step by step asking the witness a series of questions, and I asked him a number of questions for clarification and the witness was able to answer to such questions. He answered that he and his group were stopped by the Muslim army. And he also answered that both local members of the Muslim army - and I am emphasising that I'm using the words of the witness - of the Muslim army and foreigners stopped them and did the separation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This isn't the first time that there has been a difference of views between the Prosecution and Defence according to the extent to which questions are leading or not. Now, in order to avoid this type of problem in future, we should ask the witness to describe what he actually saw, and then the description provided by the witness would help us avoid jumping to conclusions and seeing what he's going to say. So either he distinguished between the members of these soldiers or not. It's very easy to lead him on, whereas the witness in fact does not say anything. So, Mr. Withopf, give great thought and skill to the way you're going to ask your questions so that the witness can answer for himself. Having said that, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness ZL, you were just informing the Trial Chamber that individuals from your group were singled out. Do you still recall who was singled out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember exactly. Two or three young guys. Otherwise, you wouldn't allowed to look. You weren't allowed to look around. Tavic Jakov and Pranjes Zdravko, I saw them. Kramar as well, Mijo and Volic Ivo. That's what I saw. I know about them. But I didn't -- I don't know about the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Witness ZL, who singled these individuals you just mentioned out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Muslims singled them out. The army, their army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After they were singled out, Witness ZL, what did happen to you? Where did you go to, if anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mehurici, the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the time when you arrived in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 11.00 or 12.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness ZL, how far is Mehurici from Maljine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 3 or 4 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where to in Mehurici, Witness ZL, were you brought to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us to the sports hall and shut us up there. They held us there in custody for 17 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who actually escorted you from Maljine to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that same army, the Muslim one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who brought you to the elementary school in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same army, soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were just informing the Trial Chamber, Witness ZL, that you were detained in the Mehurici Elementary School. Do you still recall in which area of the school you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's a hall there, a school hall. That's where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The school hall. Can you please be a bit more precise. For what purpose has the school hall used prior to being used as a detention facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was for the schoolchildren. It was -- they played their sports there inside. It was a sports hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long your detained in the sports hall of the Mehurici Elementary School?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the 8th of June to the 24th of June; 17 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many people were together with you detained in the sports hall of the Mehurici Elementary School?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 275, women, children and men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did these 275 women, children and men come from, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Maljine. There were some of them from other villages too, but most of them were from Maljine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were detained together with the 275 other people in the Mehurici Elementary School, were you guarded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether you were guarded by civilians or by soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And soldiers of which army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were detained in the Mehurici Elementary School, were there also foreign Muslims around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With us, you mean? You mean with us in the prison?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen -- to make it easier for you, Witness ZL, have you seen any foreign Muslims whilst you were detained in the Mehurici Elementary School?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, Witness ZL, when you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 24th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, can we please again go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us move into private session, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness ZL. Mr. President, Your Honours, this concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me turn towards the Defence teams for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. ZL. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you hear me and can you see me? Sir, I'm going to address you with the letters "ZL" because that is your protective name. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Edina Residovic, and I am the Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic. I should like to ask you to answer some of my questions now, please. First of all, for us to keep your identity protected, may we go into private session for me to be able to ask the witness some particulars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. ZL, you knew that for some time already there were village watches being set up around the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That morning, the 8th of June, early in the morning you first heard shots from artillery weapons, and soon after that you could hear infantry weapons too; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the spot you were at, you could notice that due to shelling or incendiary bullets several houses and sheds began to burn; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not all the sheds and houses. Just one shed and one house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, from the place you were at that morning, you were not able to see a single individual, anybody entering into somebody's house and planting a fire there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I couldn't see that. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, you could see that the hamlet of Vranjaca was set on fire, that the houses there were the ones that were burning, and Vranjaca is a hamlet of Gornje Maljine, in fact. It was where the front line was formed, facing the first part of Donje Maljine. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That part of Maljine was attacked first, both with artillery and infantry weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, the HVO lines were broken through very quickly, and some of the HVO soldiers managed to get through to the village; whereas the other portion went to the improvised field clinic set up. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You and your neighbours surrendered, and then the BH army soldiers started to form groups and told you that they would take you towards Mehurici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Could we now go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, could you raise the blinds now. According to the schedule that we have been provided with, we will be hearing two other witnesses via videolink tomorrow. Is that correct? Apparently no special measures have been requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, it's correct that we have two further videolink witnesses for tomorrow. Our colleague is still proofing the two videolink witnesses for tomorrow; therefore, we are not yet in a position to indicate as to whether there will be an application for protective measures or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Does the Defence have any other issues to raise at this point in time? Mr. Bourgon, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since we have a little time, with the Trial Chamber's leave, there are three issues we would like to raise at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The first issue concerns the order, the decision of the Chamber that relates to the consolidated exhibit list that we have received from the Prosecution, dated the 10th of March. According to the order rendered by the Trial Chamber, we have to provide our response with regard to the admissibility of each document. This should be on the 25th of March. We have started working on this. We've been doing so for a while. We have asked the Prosecution to provide us with an electronic list, and we are still waiting to receive this. We should be receiving it in a few days' time. Having said that, Mr. President, we would like to be granted additional time in order to finish our work and in order to be able to provide our response to the Trial Chamber on the 29th rather than on the 25th. This will enable us to work in a better way and to have full responses for each document concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll grant the Defence's request. You will have until Monday the 29th to state your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The second issue that we would like to raise this afternoon has to do with the documents that we have obtained from the Monitoring Mission of the European Community. As you are aware, Mr. President, we have gained access to the documents contained in the archives in Sarajevo. In the course of the last two weeks, our legal assistants have been able to examine all the documents kept in Sarajevo. We have now received copies of these documents. To be more precise, Mr. President, we have received copies of 846 documents which have been selected on the basis of criteria contained in Annex B of our initial request, our initial request for an order issued by the Trial Chamber. The problem at the moment, Mr. President, is that out of the 846 documents, it appears that a number of the documents are still missing. As an example, Mr. President, we recently verified certain matters and there are documents that we have received from the Prosecution, and these documents aren't contained in the ones that we have obtained in Sarajevo and the Monitoring Mission in 1993 should have a complete archives there. We're trying to establish why there is a difference in these two lists. We have informed the representatives of the Prosecution of our concern, and we have asked them if they could provide us with a list of the documents that they have -- not of the contents of the documents, but a list that would mention the date of the documents, the source of the documents, and the person to which the document was addressed. This would allow us to determine which documents we don't have, and that would ensure equality of arms. And my colleague has told me that this is not possible at the moment because he first has to ask for permission from the Monitoring Mission, since this is material that they obtained pursuant to Rule 70 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. So the Defence would now like to inform you that we're going to work on this and try to obtain this authorisation from the European Union Monitoring Mission in Sarajevo in order to be certain that we have the documents; that is to say, that we have the same documents that the Prosecution has, in order to ensure equality of arms when the international experts are called to testify before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. In order to summarise what you have just said, your collaborators, your assistants have gained access to the archives and in accordance with the criteria established under Annex B, they have compiled a list of 846 documents. Having examined this list, you realise that certain documents were missing and you found out that among the 846 documents there were some documents that the Prosecution had provided you with and you were surprised to see that these archives, which are supposed to contain all the documents, didn't contain all the documents. You were wondering how the Prosecution had documents that weren't in the archives. Is that what you are actually telling us?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Naturally, Mr. President, in confirmation of what we have stated, we have obtained a letter from the Monitoring Mission in Sarajevo, according to which they confirm that -- sorry, it's not 846 but 859 documents. These are the only documents contained in the Monitoring Mission archives in Sarajevo at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will now turn to Mr. Withopf. You have carefully followed what has just been said. It appears that you are in possession of certain documents, the source of which is unknown. But in any event, these documents aren't included among the 859 documents mentioned. This is the problem we are facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, of course the Prosecution has in that instance no explanation why ECMM doesn't have the documents they may have provided the Prosecution with earlier on. There may be an explanation to the extent that the Prosecution not only got ECMM documents from the ECMM but also from witnesses. In respect to the issue which has already been addressed by learned friend from the Defence, the Prosecution is certainly prepared to contact ECMM and to try to get their permission to disclose the different dates, sources, and individuals or institutions to whom such documents have been addressed to; however, as the Chamber is certainly very well aware of, all ECMM documents have been provided by ECMM on the basis of Rule 70. That implies that the Prosecution has first to ask permission by the ECMM to disclose the respective data. In that respect, I wish to use the opportunity to inform both The Chamber and Defence counsel that, as a result of the prioritised ISU searches by the Prosecution, a number of potentially Rule 68 documents have been found and such documents stem from ECMM. The Prosecution has asked permission by ECMM to disclose such documents to the Defence under Rule 68, and the deadline has been sent to ECMM. And the deadline is the 25th of March, 2004. In respect to the other issue - namely, the consolidated exhibit list - the Prosecution is prepared to provide Defence tomorrow with an electronic version of the exhibit list in order to facilitate the work of the Defence in that respect. If I may please take the opportunity, Mr. President, Your Honours, to raise a further issue; namely, the issue of the testimony and the scheduling of the Prosecution's military expert. I have contacted General Reinhardt, and the situation is the following: General Reinhardt would be available for testimony to testify between Thursday, the 29th of April and Friday, the 7th of May inclusive. Friday, the 30th of April, however, is a UN holiday. Therefore, the Prosecution suggests - and we already discussed this with Defence, which are well prepared to support the Prosecution suggestions - to make the General available from Monday, the 3rd of May until Friday, the 7th of May inclusive. Anticipating and taking into account the duration of the cross-examination as indicated by our learned friends from the Defence, the Prosecution would suggest to think about, if necessary, to have prolonged court sessions towards the end of this week to accommodate, if necessary, the full testimony of General Reinhardt, the Prosecution's military expert. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. With regard to the last issue addressed - but I'll refer to the documents in a minute - he could start testifying on Monday, the 3rd of May. I don't know whether we will be sitting in the morning or the afternoon of that week. We will check that. If we will be sitting in the morning, we'll start at 9.00 and then we could continue in the afternoon on Tuesday and Wednesday, in order to make sure that we have enough time on Friday. We'll discuss this and with the registrar we'll see if we can schedule the hearings so that on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday we work continually so that we have more time available on Friday. That's what I want to say about the schedule. I'll now go back to the issue of the documents. Naturally, the Trial Chamber has noted that the Prosecution will take this up with representatives of the European Union to see which documents can be provided. And naturally the Defence will be following this closely. If any difficulties arise, naturally you will inform the Trial Chamber of this. As far as equality of arms is concerned, it's quite natural that the Prosecution and the Defence should have equal access to documents. That's obvious. There is a third issue that you wanted to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. With regard to the third issue, I'll be very brief. The Defence has a translator/interpreter at its disposal which was assigned to the team. The translator/interpreter - it is a lady - she is involved in two matters. She enables the accused to communicate with people who don't speak B/C/S, to co-counsels, for example. And they also make it possible -- she also makes it possible for the accused to see certain documents translated into their own language. This enables them to follow the proceedings. The interpreter, when we need documents at the eleventh hour that have to be translated for the cross-examination, in such cases the interpreter also assists us. Mr. President, this is something that might be appearing in a request by the Defence. We were informed last week by the Registry that the resources won't be allocated to us to pay for this service. The Registry says that the resources for such a service should be deducted from the sum that we are already allocated. So there is a misunderstanding, as far as this subject is concerned, and we have addressed this matter in a letter to the Registry today. We are still working with this person since we need her services. This won't cause any disruptions. We'll still be in a position to continue with our work. Nevertheless, if the Registry's response is confirmed, we will then raise this issue, as you said we ought to do, in a motion filed with the Trial Chamber. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think that it's necessary to adjourn now, given the break. As we have addressed these issues -- all these issues, we will now adjourn. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00. I would like to point out that -- Yes, Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one matter which we could deal with very quickly, and it's got to do with admissibility of certain documents from a witness that was called sometime ago. It was in relation to two decisions from the Bosnian courts, one from the cantonal court in Zenica and one from the Supreme Court. Your Honours requested that the documents, which were in B/C/S, be translated in full and not only portions of the document be translated. And we have those translations now. And I would request Your Honours to accept these documents now as full translations of those two decisions. The two documents are DK7, which was marked for identification, and DK8, which was marked for identification. And our request would be that these translations replace the existing documents and that they be admitted into evidence as exhibits. At the time, there was no objection from the Prosecution regarding these documents. I have, Your Honour, copies for Your Honours and everyone else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, with respect to those documents, no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Completely correct, Mr. President. The Prosecution has no objection against tendering these documents. It's just a substitute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have marked them for identification, but we'll have a definite number in due course. The translation in English corresponds to the B/C/S text. May we have a final number, Mr. Registrar, then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, then the final numbers will be DK7 for the B/C/S version and DK7/E for the English translation; and DK8 for the B/C/S version and DK8/E for the B/C/S translation -- sorry, for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. There was just one document -- ah, two cassettes. The second was already translated; is that right? Where is the second one? Because what we actually have is this: A judgement, which has been translated -- Mr. Dixon, could you be of assistance?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: There are two decisions that have been translated. The first decision is from the cantonal court. And the second decision, which Your Honour should have, is from the Supreme Court. The first is DK7 and the second is DK8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, yes. The mistake arose from the fact that the registrar just gave us one. But you're right; we have two documents. Now, Mr. Registrar, since you were the author -- anyway, give us the numbers again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the B/C/S version of the judgement of the cantonal court gets exhibit number DK7, and the English translation of this judgement gets exhibit number DK7/E. Then the ruling of the Supreme Court of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina gets the exhibit number DK8, and the English translation gets the exhibit number DK8/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Withopf, and that will be the last speaker for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Right. And it will be very short. We just were informed, Mr. President, Your Honours, that the two witnesses who are scheduled for tomorrow won't ask for any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I thank you one and all, and we reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. The meeting is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 16th day of March, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.49 p.m.,
